hints: Focus on what water does in hydrolysis, it uses its lone pair to attack the slightly positive carbon, so think about what type of reagent that makes it.
Compare the C-Br and C-Cl bonds, remember that the weaker bond with the better leaving group breaks faster.
Put the two ideas together, the faster haloalkane plus the attack by a lone-pair donor tells you both columns of the table.
walkthrough:
**Identify the reaction type**

Think of hydrolysis as swapping the halogen for OH from water. Water acts as a nucleophile because oxygen has a lone pair to donate to the electron-poor carbon.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{X} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{HX}$$

**Decide the mechanism**

The C atom attached to the halogen is $\delta+$ because the halogen is more electronegative. A nucleophile ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) attacks it and the halide leaves, so this is nucleophilic substitution, not electrophilic substitution.

**Compare rate: C-Br vs C-Cl**

Bond strength is the key. The $\text{C-Br}$ bond is longer and weaker than the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond, so it needs less energy to break. $\text{Br}^-$ is also a larger, more stable ion, so it is a better leaving group than $\text{Cl}^-$.

Bond enthalpy idea:
$$E(\text{C-Br}) < E(\text{C-Cl})$$

**Conclude the faster compound**

Because its bond breaks more easily, bromoethane hydrolyses more rapidly than chloroethane. Faster compound plus nucleophilic substitution gives the correct row.

options.A: Half right and half wrong. Bromoethane is indeed faster, but electrophilic substitution is incorrect. Electrophiles attack electron-rich areas, while here water donates a lone pair to the $\delta+$ carbon, which is nucleophilic attack.
options.B: Correct on both parts. Bromoethane is faster because the C-Br bond is weaker than C-Cl and Br- is the better leaving group. The mechanism is nucleophilic substitution by water to form ethanol.
options.C: Wrong on both parts. Chloroethane is slower because the C-Cl bond is stronger and harder to break. Electrophilic substitution is also wrong, as this reaction involves nucleophilic attack by water.
options.D: The mechanism is correct but the compound is wrong. Many students pick chloroethane thinking chlorine is more electronegative so it should be more reactive. In halogenoalkanes, rate depends on bond strength and leaving group ability, not electronegativity, so bromoethane wins.
